entities.summary:
Arnold (Arnoul) of Soissons, also known as Arnold or Arnulf of Oudenburg (c. 1040 – 1087), was a Benedictine monk, abbot, and eventually Bishop of Soissons, whose enduring legacy stems from his posthumous veneration as the patron saint of hop-pickers and Belgian brewers. Born in Brabant, likely Tiegem, within the historical County of Flanders, Arnold's life spanned a period of significant monastic reform and ecclesiastical consolidation in Western Europe, placing him at the intersection of spiritual devotion and practical community life in the 11th century.

Initially a knight, Arnold renounced military life to enter the Benedictine monastery of Saint-Médard in Soissons, France, where he quickly distinguished himself through his piety and learning. His monastic career saw him rise to abbot of Saint-Médard and, in 1080, he was reluctantly consecrated Bishop of Soissons. His episcopate was marked by efforts to restore discipline and resolve conflicts within the diocese, often acting as a peacemaker during a turbulent era. Dissatisfied with the political demands of his episcopal office, Arnold eventually sought and received permission from Pope Gregory VII to resign his see, retreating to a hermitage. He subsequently founded the Abbey of Saint Peter in Oudenburg, Flanders, around 1084, serving as its first abbot until his death in 1087.
